set1.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
set1.q: In a patient with a post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70, a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 42% predicted corresponds to which airflow grade?
opts: Grade 1, mild, requires 80% predicted or more. At 42% this patient is far below it. Tell: grade 1 is the only grade with near-normal airflow. Mild airflow limitation means near-normal airflow.
Grade 2, moderate, covers 50% up to 80% predicted. At 42% this patient is below the 50% line. Tell: under 50% moves the grade to severe. Grade 2 covers 50% to 79% predicted only.
Correct. Grade 3, severe, covers a post-bronchodilator 1-second volume of 30% up to 50% predicted, so 42% falls there. Grade 2 starts at 50% and grade 4 is below 30%.
Grade 4, very severe, is below 30% predicted. At 42% this patient is above that line. Tell: 30% to 49% is grade 3. Very severe means less than a third of predicted airflow.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: Which statement about albuterol in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is accurate?
opts: Albuterol is the rescue inhaler; long-acting bronchodilators treat ongoing bronchoconstriction and prevent exacerbations. Tell: groups B and E need long-acting therapy alongside it.

Correct. Every patient should have an albuterol inhaler to prevent or reduce symptoms, as needed. It should not be used excessively, because of toxicity and the risk of cardiac and psychiatric side effects.
It is reserved for severe disease
Albuterol is for every patient, from group A onward, to prevent or reduce symptoms. Tell: rescue medicine is universal; what changes with severity is the long-acting regimen.
Excessive use carries toxicity and the risk of cardiac and psychiatric side effects. Tell: heavy rescue use is a warning sign, and discharge requires needing it no more often than every 4 hours.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: An acute exacerbation is defined as worsening dyspnea, cough or sputum developing over how many days or fewer?
opts: Three days is too narrow; the definition allows worsening over up to 14 days. Tell: a decline that builds over a week or two still counts as an exacerbation.
Seven days is too short a window; the definition is worsening over 14 days or less. Tell: the number is 2 weeks. Worsening across 8 to 14 days still meets the definition.

Correct. An acute exacerbation is an acute worsening of dyspnea, cough or sputum over 14 days or less, triggered by viral or bacterial infection or pollution. Pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, acute heart failure and pneumothorax must be excluded.
A month is longer than the definition, which is worsening over 14 days or less. Tell: slow change over a month is progression to evaluate, not the acute event defined here.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: What is the primary risk factor for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: A sedentary lifestyle with limited activity is listed among risk factors, but it is not the primary one. Tell: the dominant risk is inhaled tobacco smoke, which is why smoking cessation can slow progression.

Correct. Tobacco smoking or exposure is the primary risk factor, behind about 90% of cases. Secondary risks are biomass burning, occupational dusts and fumes, a sedentary lifestyle and, much more rarely, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
Burning wood or coal indoors for cooking and heating is a secondary risk factor, larger in developing countries. Tell: worldwide, the primary risk factor is tobacco smoking or exposure.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic risk found even in nonsmokers, but it is rare, about 3 or 4 cases per 10,000. Tell: it is evaluated in young or unexposed patients, while tobacco remains the primary cause.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: Which adverse effect is the main one for long-acting antimuscarinic antagonists such as tiotropium?
opts: Correct. Long-acting antimuscarinics block M3 receptors to limit bronchoconstriction and help prevent exacerbations, with mild help in reducing sputum. Absorption is poor, so adverse effects are limited, mainly to dry mouth.
Tachycardia and arrhythmias come from the sympathetic stimulation of long-acting beta agonists. Tell: antimuscarinics are poorly absorbed, so their main effect is local, dry mouth.

Pneumonia risk rises with inhaled corticosteroids. Tell: tiotropium is a bronchodilator with limited, mostly local side effects, chiefly dry mouth. That risk belongs to the steroid, not the bronchodilator.

Weight gain and bruising are systemic corticosteroid effects. Tell: tiotropium's poor absorption leaves dry mouth as its main adverse effect. Those come with oral steroids, used for exacerbations only.

set1.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
set1.q: Which test result separates emphysema from chronic bronchitis and asthma?
opts: A raised bicarbonate reflects compensation for chronic carbon dioxide retention, which comes earlier in chronic bronchitis. Tell: emphysema is singled out by a reduced diffusing capacity.

Correct. The diffusing capacity is reduced in emphysema, because destroyed alveoli and bullae limit gas transfer, separating it from chronic bronchitis (normal or near normal) and asthma. Spirometry alone cannot tell emphysema from chronic bronchitis.
A post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70 confirms obstruction in both subtypes. Tell: it shows that the disease is present, not which subtype dominates.
A small bronchodilator response marks irreversible obstruction, shared by both subtypes. Tell: the measurement that singles out alveolar destruction is diffusing capacity.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: Which finding is one of the discharge criteria after an exacerbation?
opts: Albuterol no more than every 4 hours

Correct. Discharge criteria include needing inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist no more often than every 4 hours, using long-acting bronchodilators, walking across the room if previously ambulatory, eating and sleeping without frequent waking, and clinical stability for 12 to 24 hours.
Spirometry stays obstructed in this disease, so normal spirometry is not a discharge criterion. Tell: discharge rests on rescue use, stability, mobility and a home plan.
Climbing a full flight of stairs
The criterion is walking across the room if previously ambulatory, not climbing stairs. Tell: the bar is basic mobility, eating and sleep without frequent waking.
Clinical stability for 12 to 24 hours is required, not 72. Tell: the stated window is 12 to 24 hours. A patient stable for a day can go home if the other criteria are met.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)/ chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD) for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
set1.q: What is noted about pulmonary rehabilitation referral for older adults?
opts: It serves just a return to work
Return to work is the rehabilitation aim listed for working-age adults; older adults gain function and fewer admissions. Tell: for older adults the point is active referral.
They are referred less, so refer actively
Correct. Older adults are less often referred for rehabilitation, so the advice is to refer them actively. For younger adults, rehabilitation aims at a return to work and activity.
Nothing restricts rehabilitation by age; the problem is that older adults are referred less often. Tell: the advice is to refer them actively. Older adults benefit from rehabilitation as well.
Rehabilitation reduces dyspnea, improves exercise tolerance and cuts hospitalizations, benefits that matter for older adults too. Tell: the gap is under-referral, which clinicians should correct.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: What is the main role of the chest x-ray in this disease?
opts: The diagnosis is confirmed only by spirometry, with a post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70. Tell: the x-ray supports the picture and excludes mimics, but it cannot confirm obstruction.

Airflow obstruction is graded from the post-bronchodilator 1-second volume as a percent of predicted. Tell: imaging cannot measure airflow. Grades come from spirometry: 80% or more is grade 1, under 30% is grade 4.
Air trapping is measured by lung volumes, a raised residual volume. Tell: the x-ray can suggest hyperinflation, but its main job is excluding other diagnoses.

Correct. The chest x-ray is not a diagnostic standard, but it can rule out other diagnoses such as heart failure or pneumothorax and may show overinflated hyperlucent lungs, a flattened diaphragm, bullae or a narrow vertical heart.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: In the Five A's approach to behavior change, which step comes right after Advise?
opts: Assist is the fourth step, helping set actionable goals and strategies, and it follows the readiness check. Tell: Assess comes between Advise and Assist.
Ask is the first step, opening the discussion about the behavior before any advice is given. Tell: the order is Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange. Asking opens the conversation nonjudgmentally.

Correct. The Five A's run Ask (open a nonjudgmental conversation), Advise (clear, tailored advice), Assess (readiness and willingness to change), Assist (realistic steps and strategies) and Arrange (follow-up to monitor progress).
Arrange is the fifth and last step, setting up follow-up to monitor progress and keep motivation. Tell: after advising, the clinician first assesses whether the person is ready to change.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: Long-term supplemental oxygen is indicated when the resting arterial oxygen pressure falls below which value?
opts: Correct. Supplemental oxygen is indicated when the arterial oxygen pressure is below 55 mmHg or the saturation below 88%, and it is proven to decrease the risk of death, prolong life and improve quality of life.
A threshold of 65 mmHg is too high; the indication is a pressure below 55 mmHg or saturation below 88%. Tell: oxygen treats severe resting hypoxemia, not mild lowering.
A threshold of 75 mmHg would treat many patients without severe resting hypoxemia. Tell: the line is below 55 mmHg. That value is well above the severe hypoxemia that oxygen treats.
A threshold of 85 mmHg is near normal and far above the indication. Tell: long-term oxygen starts below 55 mmHg or a saturation below 88%. Such a patient has no resting hypoxemia.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)/ chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD) for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
set1.q: Which care priority is listed for adults aged about 40 to 64 rather than for older adults?
opts: Correct. For adults about 40 to 64 the priorities are smoking cessation, preserving lung function, staying in work and preventing exacerbations. For adults 65 and older they shift to function, quality of life, multimorbidity and goals of care.
Goals of care are a priority for adults 65 and older, along with function, quality of life and multimorbidity. Tell: working-age adults focus on staying in work and preserving lung function.
Multimorbidity is an elderly priority, as osteoporosis, frailty, falls and cognitive decline join heart disease and depression. Tell: the working-age list includes staying in work.
Quality of life is listed among priorities for adults 65 and older. Tell: for the 40 to 64 group the list centers on cessation, lung function, work and exacerbation prevention.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: Which measurement is one of the 4 inputs of the BODE (body mass index, obstruction, dyspnea, exercise) index?
opts: Correct. The index scores body mass index, airflow obstruction (1-second volume, percent predicted), dyspnea (the modified Medical Research Council grade) and exercise capacity, measured as the 6-minute walk distance, to estimate 4-year survival.
Arterial carbon dioxide describes gas exchange in exacerbations and is not scored in the index. Tell: the exercise input is the 6-minute walk distance.
Diffusing capacity flags emphysema but is not one of the 4 inputs. Tell: obstruction in the index is measured by the 1-second volume, and exercise by the walk test.
The symptom assessment test helps set the treatment group. Tell: the dyspnea input of the survival index is the modified Medical Research Council grade, and exercise is the walk distance.

set1.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
set1.q: Under the current three-group scheme, a patient at high exacerbation risk is placed in which group regardless of symptoms?
opts: Group B is low risk with more symptoms. Tell: B still requires low exacerbation risk; any high-risk patient is E. Group B starts on a long-acting beta agonist plus a long-acting antimuscarinic.
Group D belongs to the 2020 four-group scheme (high risk, more symptoms). Tell: the current scheme merged C and D into E. A high-risk patient today is E, whatever the symptom score.

Correct. In the 2023/2026 scheme, low-risk patients are group A or B by symptoms, and any high-risk patient (2 or more moderate exacerbations or 1 hospitalization) is group E, which combines the old groups C and D.
Group A is low risk with fewer symptoms (dyspnea grade 0 to 1, assessment score under 10). Tell: high exacerbation risk overrides symptoms and means group E.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: Which feature belongs to the chronic bronchitis subtype rather than emphysema?
opts: Correct. In the chronic bronchitis subtype, airway narrowing and mucus plugging bring earlier hypoxemia and hypercapnia, with cough, sputum, rhonchi and possible cyanosis and edema. In emphysema, gas exchange is relatively preserved until late.
Relatively preserved gas exchange until late disease is the emphysema pattern. Tell: chronic bronchitis is the subtype with early hypoxemia and hypercapnia, which fits its cyanosis and edema.

A reduced diffusing capacity marks emphysema, from destroyed alveoli; in chronic bronchitis it is normal or near normal. Tell: the diffusing capacity is the test that separates emphysema from chronic bronchitis.
Hyperinflation, flat diaphragms and bullae are emphysema imaging findings. Tell: imaging in chronic bronchitis shows bronchial wall thickening, the airway-centered change.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: Why is a complete blood count part of the workup for this disease?
opts: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a separate level, diagnostic below 11 micromol/L with a deficient genotype. Tell: the blood count checks anemia and eosinophils.
Suspected heart failure is checked with B-type natriuretic peptide, not the blood count. Tell: the blood count's 2 targets are anemia and eosinophils.
To find anemia and count eosinophils

Correct. The complete blood count checks for coincident anemia and measures eosinophils; an elevated eosinophil count is when adding an inhaled corticosteroid is considered. Anemia is also on the comorbidity screening list.
No blood test confirms the disease; spirometry does, with a post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70. Tell: the blood count looks for anemia and eosinophils.

set1.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
set1.q: Which test is required to establish the diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: An arterial blood gas is usually done only in a deteriorating or severe exacerbation, where it shows chronic carbon dioxide retention. Tell: it describes gas exchange; spirometry confirms the diagnosis.

Correct. Spirometry, the cornerstone test, is required to establish the diagnosis and is done before and after a bronchodilator such as albuterol. A post-bronchodilator ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity below 0.70 confirms it.

The chest x-ray is not a diagnostic standard; it rules out other diagnoses such as heart failure or pneumothorax and may show hyperinflation or bullae. Tell: only spirometry can show the persistent obstruction that defines the disease.
Chest computed tomography can help categorize emphysema but is generally not needed. Tell: the diagnosis rests on spirometry before and after a bronchodilator, not on imaging.

set1.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
set1.q: In the emphysema subtype, what causes the airways to obstruct?
opts: Airway narrowing and mucus plugging are the chronic bronchitis mechanism, from mucus gland hyperplasia and wall thickening. Tell: emphysema obstructs because the recoil that holds airways open is lost.
Allergen-triggered bronchospasm that reverses is extrinsic asthma. Tell: emphysema's obstruction comes from destroyed alveoli and lost elastic recoil, so it does not reverse.
A stiff chest wall limiting inspiration is a restrictive problem, the opposite of this disease. Tell: emphysema limits expiration as airways collapse, causing air trapping and hyperinflation.

Correct. Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, and the loss of elastic recoil lets the airways collapse on expiration, trapping air. In chronic bronchitis, obstruction instead comes from airway narrowing and mucus plugging.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: Which laboratory finding prompts consideration of adding an inhaled corticosteroid?
opts: A low alpha-1 antitrypsin with a deficient genotype diagnoses the deficiency behind emphysema in young patients or those with few exposures. Tell: the inhaled corticosteroid decision rests on eosinophils.
B-type natriuretic peptide is checked when heart failure is suspected. Tell: eosinophils, measured on the blood count, are what prompt an inhaled corticosteroid.

Correct. For group E, a long-acting beta agonist plus antimuscarinic is the start, with an inhaled corticosteroid considered when blood eosinophils are 300 or more; at discharge after an exacerbation, an inhaled corticosteroid is considered if eosinophils are elevated.
A raised bicarbonate reflects compensation for chronic carbon dioxide retention. Tell: the laboratory value that guides inhaled corticosteroid use is the blood eosinophil count.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: Next to smoking cessation, which therapy tends to be the most effective management for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: Oral corticosteroids are for acute exacerbations only in this disease. Tell: rehabilitation is the effective long-term therapy after cessation. They are not used for long-term care.

Correct. Next to smoking cessation, pulmonary rehabilitation tends to be the most effective therapy, reducing dyspnea, improving exercise tolerance and mobility, and reducing hospitalizations and readmissions. It needs a healthcare professional or team.

Inhaled corticosteroids are used only with a long-acting beta agonist and raise pneumonia risk. Tell: rehabilitation, which trains breathing, secretion clearance and strength, ranks just behind cessation.
Long-term azithromycin is used rarely and increases resistance and side effects. Tell: the second most effective management is pulmonary rehabilitation.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: Smoking-related emphysema typically follows which pattern?
opts: Panlobular emphysema in the lower lobes is the alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency pattern. Tell: smoking damages the upper lobes in a centrilobular pattern.

Bronchial wall thickening is the imaging change of chronic bronchitis, an airway disease, not an emphysema pattern. Tell: smoking-related emphysema destroys centrilobular airspaces in the upper lobes.
Fibrosis is a restrictive change and, with silica or fiberglass, a different condition. Tell: smoking-related emphysema is an obstructive, upper-lobe, centrilobular destruction of airspaces.

Correct. Emphysema from smoking is centrilobular and predominantly in the upper lobes. The panlobular, lower-lobe pattern belongs to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, which is why basilar emphysema prompts testing for it.

set1.io: Identify medical care strategies for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)/ chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD) for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
set1.q: A patient's disease is severe, with a forced expiratory volume in 1 second below 40% predicted. When should the pneumococcal vaccine be given?
opts: Age 65 is the default timing, but severe disease below 40% or cardiac comorbidity moves vaccination earlier. Tell: severity, not age, sets the timing here.
Vaccination is preventive and is given when the severe disease is recognized, not deferred to an exacerbation. Tell: the earlier timing exists to reduce pneumonia before it happens.
Delaying past 75 is later than even the default of 65. Tell: severe disease (below 40%) or cardiac comorbidity calls for vaccination as soon as that severity is recognized.

Correct. Every patient should receive the pneumococcal vaccine at age 65, but those with severe disease (1-second volume below 40%) or cardiac comorbidities should get it earlier, essentially when diagnosed and recognized at that severity.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: Which body habitus statement about patients with this disease is accurate?
opts: Weight gain in these patients usually reflects inactivity because breathlessness limits movement, not improving lungs. Tell: gaining weight can be a sign of worsening function.

Correct. Patients are not always thin; they may be overweight, obese or gaining weight because breathlessness keeps them inactive. The thin pursed-lip breather is a classic emphysema picture, not a rule for everyone.
They are thin in every case
Thinness is the classic emphysema descriptor, but patients may be overweight or gaining weight from inactivity. Tell: weight does not exclude the disease.
Inactivity from dyspnea can lead to weight gain even with emphysema. Tell: body habitus is a classic picture, not a diagnostic criterion; spirometry confirms the disease.

set1.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
set1.q: Which lung volume change reflects air trapping in this disease?
opts: Residual volume rises, not falls, as air is trapped behind narrowed and collapsing airways. Tell: trapping means more air left in the lungs after expiration.
Total lung capacity rises with hyperinflation; a reduced total lung capacity confirms restriction instead. Tell: obstruction inflates the lungs, restriction shrinks them.

Functional residual capacity rises with hyperinflation in this disease. Tell: every volume affected by trapping goes up, not down. A reduced functional residual capacity would suggest restriction instead.
Correct. Air trapping raises the residual volume, and hyperinflation raises total lung capacity and functional residual capacity. With exertion, dynamic hyperinflation worsens and drives dyspnea.

set1.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
set1.q: Spirometry shows obstruction and the forced vital capacity is also low, raising the possibility of a mixed disorder. Which measurement confirms it?
opts: Diffusing capacity is reduced in emphysema and separates it from chronic bronchitis and asthma. Tell: it does not measure lung size, so it cannot confirm restriction.
The bronchodilator response tells reversible from irreversible obstruction. Tell: the question of added restriction is answered by total lung capacity.
An arterial blood gas measures oxygen and carbon dioxide and is usually kept for deteriorating or severe exacerbations. Tell: restriction is a volume question, answered by total lung capacity.

Correct. When an obstructed study also has a low forced vital capacity, a mixed obstructive and restrictive disorder is possible and is confirmed with total lung capacity. Lung volumes identify hyperinflation or coexisting restriction.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: Which statement about sputum production in this disease is accurate?
opts: Correct. Patients do not always produce sputum: it is seen with chronic bronchitis or a combined presentation and is typically not prevalent in emphysema-only cases. Its absence does not exclude the disease.
It is present in every patient
Sputum is not universal; emphysema-only patients typically do not produce much. Tell: sputum reflects mucus hypersecretion from the chronic bronchitis component.
It is typical of pure emphysema
Emphysema-only cases typically lack prominent sputum; mucus hypersecretion is the chronic bronchitis pattern. Tell: the thin, pursed-lip breather has dyspnea more than sputum.
Its absence rules out the disease
Patients do not always have sputum, so its absence cannot exclude the disease, especially emphysema. Tell: spirometry, not sputum, confirms the diagnosis.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: Where can most exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease be managed?
opts: Intensive care is for hemodynamic instability, major infection or need for invasive ventilation, a small minority. Tell: most exacerbations, more than 80%, are managed outpatient.
Admission follows specific criteria such as marked symptoms despite treatment or need for noninvasive ventilation. Tell: the majority of exacerbations stay outpatient.
Rehabilitation is considered after an exacerbation as part of the discharge bundle, not as the place to treat one. Tell: most exacerbations are treated as outpatients.

Correct. More than 80% of exacerbations can be managed as outpatients after triage of severity. Admission is reserved for marked symptoms despite acute management, need for noninvasive ventilation, new signs, arrhythmia, poor secretion control, comorbidities or lack of home support.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: Which emphysema pattern does alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency cause?
opts: Bronchial wall thickening is the imaging change of the chronic bronchitis subtype, not an emphysema pattern. Tell: the deficiency destroys alveoli across whole lobules in the lower lobes.
Isolated large bullae in the apex
Bullae can appear in emphysema, but an apical location is not the deficiency pattern. Tell: the deficiency is defined by panlobular emphysema concentrated at the lung bases.

Correct. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes panlobular emphysema predominantly in the lower lobes, which shows as basilar emphysema on the chest x-ray. Smoking causes centrilobular emphysema in the upper lobes.
Centrilobular emphysema in the upper lobes is the smoking pattern. Tell: the deficiency is the lower-lobe, panlobular pattern, a clue that points to testing in a young or nonsmoking patient.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: How do bullae differ from blebs?
opts: Bullae occur in asthma, blebs in emphysema
Both blebs and bullae come from airspace destruction, the emphysema process. Tell: asthma does not destroy alveoli; the difference between the two is how deep and how large they are.
Bullae lie deeper and grow larger

Correct. Blebs arise from destroyed airspaces and are not contained by the connective tissue of the visceral pleura, while bullae develop deep to the internal elastic layer, form their own sacs within connective tissue, and become significantly bigger than blebs.
Bullae lie under the pleura and stay small
That describes blebs, which form beneath the visceral pleura and stay smaller. Tell: bullae are the deeper and much larger air pockets. Bullae form their own sacs deep to the internal elastic layer.
Both are air pockets from destroyed airspaces, also called pneumatosis, and they limit diffusing capacity. Tell: what separates them is depth and size, not contents.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set1.q: Under the current three-group scheme, which initial pharmacologic treatment fits group B?
opts: One bronchodilator is the start for group A, with few symptoms. Tell: group B has more symptoms, which calls for both long-acting bronchodilators. A single agent leaves a symptomatic patient undertreated.
Inhaled corticosteroids are never used alone in this disease and raise pneumonia risk. Tell: group B starts on the 2 long-acting bronchodilators. They must be paired with a long-acting beta agonist.
Oral corticosteroids are for acute exacerbations only in this disease, not chronic treatment. Tell: group B's maintenance is a long-acting beta agonist plus antimuscarinic.

Correct. Group B, more symptoms (dyspnea grade 2 or more, or assessment score 10 or more) with low exacerbation risk, starts on a long-acting beta agonist plus a long-acting antimuscarinic. A single combined inhaler may be more convenient and effective.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: Which chest x-ray finding fits chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: Correct. The chest x-ray may show overinflated lungs with hyperlucent fields, a flattened diaphragm, bullae or blebs, and a narrow or vertical heart when heart failure is absent. The flat diaphragm reflects hyperinflation.
Hyperinflation pushes the diaphragm down and flattens it. Tell: an elevated diaphragm is the opposite of what overinflated lungs produce. The x-ray instead shows hyperlucent, overinflated fields.
The lungs are overinflated with hyperlucent fields, not small. Tell: low lung volumes point to restriction, the opposite of this disease's air trapping.
The heart tends to look narrow or vertical between overinflated lungs when heart failure is absent. Tell: hyperinflation stretches the chest vertically and narrows the heart shadow.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)/ chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD) for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
set2.q: Which diagnostic caution applies to adults 65 and older with suspected chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: The concern runs the other way: the fixed 0.70 ratio may overdiagnose older adults. Tell: overall the disease is underdiagnosed, but in the elderly the fixed ratio overcalls it.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin testing targets the young or those with few exposures. Tell: in older adults the caution is that the fixed ratio may overdiagnose.

Correct. In older adults the fixed 0.70 ratio may overdiagnose, so the clinical context is weighed. In adults under 50, lower limits of normal or z-scores help, and in the young or minimally exposed, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is considered.
Spirometry still confirms the diagnosis in older adults; the caution is about interpreting the fixed ratio. Tell: the risk in the elderly is overdiagnosis from the 0.70 cutoff.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: What is the primary site of disease in the emphysema subtype?
opts: Correct. Emphysema involves the respiratory bronchioles and alveoli, where alveolar walls are destroyed and airspaces enlarge. The chronic bronchitis subtype instead centers on the large and small airways, with mucus gland hyperplasia, goblet cells and wall thickening.

Mucus gland hyperplasia in the large and small airways is the chronic bronchitis subtype, which causes mucus hypersecretion. Tell: emphysema is a disease of the distal lung, the respiratory bronchioles and alveoli.
The pleura is not the primary site, although blebs can form beneath the visceral pleura. Tell: the destruction in emphysema is in the alveolar walls and respiratory bronchioles.
The pulmonary circulation is not the primary site; right heart strain (cor pulmonale) is a consequence, not the lesion. Tell: emphysema destroys the alveoli and respiratory bronchioles.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: When is an arterial blood gas usually obtained in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: Correct. An arterial blood gas is usually done only in a deteriorating or severely exacerbated patient, where it typically shows chronic hypercapnia above 45 mmHg. Stable outpatients are diagnosed and followed with spirometry.

Routine stable visits use symptoms, exacerbation history and spirometry, not arterial punctures. Tell: blood gases are for the acutely worse patient. Stable patients are followed with spirometry and symptoms.
Spirometry confirms the diagnosis with a post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70. Tell: the blood gas describes gas exchange in an acute decline, not whether the disease is present.
Inhaler choice comes from the patient's group, built from symptoms and exacerbation risk. Tell: an arterial blood gas is saved for deteriorating or severe exacerbations.

set2.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
set2.q: In the 2020 four-group scheme, a patient with few symptoms and high exacerbation risk belongs to which group?
opts: Group D is high symptoms with high risk. Tell: with few symptoms, a high-risk patient is C, not D. Group D needs both more symptoms and high risk; this patient has the risk without the symptom burden.

Correct. In the 2020 scheme, symptoms times risk gives the group: low symptoms and low risk is A, high symptoms and low risk is B, low symptoms and high risk is C, and high symptoms and high risk is D.
Group A is low symptoms with low risk. Tell: high exacerbation risk moves a low-symptom patient up to C. Group A means few symptoms and no more than 1 exacerbation without admission.
Group B is high symptoms with low risk. Tell: this patient has few symptoms and high risk, the opposite corner of the grid. Group B has more symptoms (dyspnea grade 2 or more) with low risk.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: A raised serum bicarbonate together with a raised arterial carbon dioxide pressure in this disease reflects what?
opts: A sign of new kidney failure
The raised bicarbonate is explained by compensation for chronic hypercapnia, not by kidney disease. Tell: the pairing of high carbon dioxide and high bicarbonate is the expected compensated pattern.

Correct. Blood gases usually show chronic hypercapnia, with arterial carbon dioxide above 45 mmHg, and the metabolic panel may show a raised bicarbonate. The combination shows a compensatory metabolic alkalosis for the chronic carbon dioxide retention.
A metabolic acidosis lowers bicarbonate; here bicarbonate is raised. Tell: a high bicarbonate with chronic carbon dioxide retention is compensation, a metabolic alkalosis.
A respiratory alkalosis lowers carbon dioxide; these patients retain it, above 45 mmHg. Tell: raised carbon dioxide with raised bicarbonate is chronic retention with metabolic compensation.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: Which treatment is the only one that can slow the progression of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: Inhaled corticosteroids are used with a long-acting beta agonist to reduce exacerbations and raise pneumonia risk; they do not halt the disease. Tell: the one intervention that slows progression is removing the smoke.

Rehabilitation is the most effective therapy after smoking cessation, reducing dyspnea and hospitalizations, but it improves function rather than slowing progression. Tell: cessation is ranked first because only it slows the disease.

Correct. Smoking cessation, with limiting exposure to triggers, is the only treatment that can slow progression; other treatments target symptom palliation and fewer hospitalizations. It is also why the disease is preventable in almost all cases.

Long-acting bronchodilators treat bronchoconstriction and help prevent exacerbations, improving the 1-second volume slightly. Tell: drug treatment palliates symptoms and cuts hospitalizations, but only stopping exposure slows decline.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: Which condition should patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease be screened for as a comorbidity?
opts: Allergic rhinitis is part of the atopic picture of extrinsic asthma. Tell: the comorbidities to screen for in this disease include osteoporosis, anemia and skeletal muscle dysfunction.

Correct. Comorbidities to screen for include cardiovascular disease, lung cancer, osteoporosis, anxiety and depression, reflux disease, anemia and skeletal muscle dysfunction. Osteoporosis matters even more in the elderly, along with frailty and falls.

Atopic dermatitis belongs to the atopic triad with allergic rhinitis and asthma, not to this disease's comorbidity list. Tell: the screening list here includes osteoporosis, heart disease, lung cancer, anemia and depression.
Nasal polyps are common in intrinsic asthma, not a listed comorbidity here. Tell: patients with this disease are screened for osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease, lung cancer and mood disorders.

set2.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
set2.q: Which post-bronchodilator ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity confirms the diagnosis when the value falls below it?
opts: A cutoff of 0.50 would miss many patients with real obstruction, since every ratio between 0.50 and 0.70 is already abnormal. Tell: the confirming threshold is below 0.70.
A cutoff of 0.60 is too low and would miss obstruction in the 0.60 to 0.70 range. Tell: the diagnosis is confirmed by a post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70.

Correct. A post-bronchodilator ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity below 0.70 confirms the diagnosis. In older adults this fixed ratio may overdiagnose, so clinical context is weighed.
A cutoff of 0.80 would label many people without obstruction as diseased. Tell: the number to remember is 0.70, measured after the bronchodilator. A ratio between 0.70 and 0.80 is not diagnostic.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: Which adverse effect is the main risk of long-acting beta agonists in this disease?
opts: Correct. Long-acting beta agonists treat ongoing bronchoconstriction and help prevent exacerbations, but their sympathetic stimulation can cause tachycardia and other cardiac effects, including arrhythmias, and can make atrial fibrillation worse.
Dry mouth is the main adverse effect of long-acting antimuscarinics, whose poor absorption keeps side effects limited. Tell: beta agonists stimulate the sympathetic system, so their risk is cardiac.
Pneumonia risk rises with inhaled corticosteroids, which must be combined with a long-acting beta agonist. Tell: the beta agonist's own risk is sympathetic: tachycardia and arrhythmias.
Fracture risk in older adults is tied to inhaled corticosteroids. Tell: long-acting beta agonists carry cardiac risk, such as worsening atrial fibrillation.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: Which occupational exposure is listed as raising the risk of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease itself, rather than of a different lung condition?
opts: Correct. Occupational risk comes from coal dust, gold mining, welding and other fumes such as textiles. Silica and fiberglass also increase risk but lead to other conditions (silicosis, fibrosis and pneumoconiosis).
Silica exposure increases risk but leads to silicosis, a different condition. Tell: coal dust, gold mining, welding and textile fumes are the exposures listed for this disease itself.

Fiberglass is grouped with silica as an exposure that results in other conditions, fibrosis or pneumoconiosis. Tell: the occupational exposures tied to this disease are coal dust, gold mining, welding and fumes.

Cat dander is an inhaled allergen that activates mast cells in allergic asthma; it is not an occupational cause of this disease. Tell: occupational risk here comes from dusts and fumes such as coal, gold mining and welding.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: What should patients be told about recovery after an exacerbation?
opts: A few days understates recovery, which can take 4 to 6 weeks. Tell: setting realistic expectations is part of discharge education. Patients told a few days may think a slower recovery means failure.
One to 2 weeks is shorter than the stated timeline of 4 to 6 weeks. Tell: patients may also not return fully to baseline. Recovery can last a month or more.

Correct. Discharge education covers the recovery timeline: recovery can take 4 to 6 weeks, and the patient may not return to baseline. The bundle also starts long-acting bronchodilators promptly, checks inhaler technique and arranges follow-up.
Six months overstates the usual course, which is 4 to 6 weeks. Tell: the realistic expectation is about a month or more, possibly without a full return to baseline.

set2.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
set2.q: In a patient with a post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70, a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 64% predicted corresponds to which airflow grade?
opts: Grade 1, mild, needs 80% predicted or more. At 64% this patient is below it. Tell: anything from 50% to 79% is grade 2. At 64%, the limitation is moderate, not mild.
Correct. Grade 2, moderate, covers a post-bronchodilator 1-second volume of 50% up to 80% predicted, so 64% falls there. Grade 1 needs 80% or more, and grade 3 begins below 50%.
Grade 3, severe, covers 30% to 49% predicted. At 64% this patient is above the 50% line. Tell: severe starts below 50%. At 64%, this patient sits 14 points above the severe range.
Grade 4, very severe, is below 30% predicted, far under this patient's 64%. Tell: very severe means less than a third of predicted airflow. That cutoff is 30%, less than half of this patient's value.

set2.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
set2.q: Which laboratory result is diagnostic of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency?
opts: Eosinophils are measured on the blood count and guide whether an inhaled corticosteroid is considered. Tell: they say nothing about the deficiency, which is diagnosed by a low enzyme level and genotype.
B-type natriuretic peptide is checked when associated heart failure is suspected. Tell: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is diagnosed by a low enzyme level with a severely deficient genotype.

Correct. An alpha-1 antitrypsin level below 11 micromol/L together with a severely deficient genotype is diagnostic. Testing is aimed at young, unexposed or basilar-emphysema patients, or those with a family history.

A raised bicarbonate on the metabolic panel reflects compensation for chronic carbon dioxide retention, not the deficiency. Tell: the diagnosis needs the enzyme level itself, below 11 micromol/L, with a deficient genotype.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: Which oral antibiotic is chosen in an exacerbation when Pseudomonas is a concern?
opts: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is an option for uncomplicated exacerbations. Tell: pseudomonal concern moves the choice to levofloxacin. It covers the uncomplicated organisms, not Pseudomonas.
Azithromycin, a macrolide, is an uncomplicated-exacerbation option and is very active against atypical organisms. Tell: it is not the pseudomonal choice; levofloxacin is.

Correct. Uncomplicated cases use doxycycline, a macrolide, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or amoxicillin-clavulanate; with resistance, a respiratory fluoroquinolone is considered, and levofloxacin is chosen for pseudomonal concern.
Doxycycline is an option for uncomplicated exacerbations caused by Haemophilus influenzae, streptococci or other gram-positive organisms. Tell: it does not cover Pseudomonas; levofloxacin does.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: When should antibiotics be given in an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: Wheezing reflects bronchoconstriction, treated with bronchodilators. Tell: antibiotics follow increased sputum volume and purulence with breathlessness.
Antibiotic timing is set by the sputum change, not a fixed wait. Tell: shortness of breath with increased, purulent sputum is the indication from the start.
With more, and more purulent, sputum

Correct. Antibiotics are given when the patient is short of breath with increased sputum volume and purulence over baseline. Uncomplicated cases use oral doxycycline, a macrolide, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or amoxicillin-clavulanate.
Exacerbations can be triggered by viruses or pollution, and antibiotics are tied to a specific sputum change. Tell: the trigger for antibiotics is more sputum that is also more purulent.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: Which approach increases the efficacy of any smoking cessation attempt?
opts: Medicines such as nicotine replacement, bupropion and varenicline help, but cessation attempts should all be combined with counseling. Tell: drug therapy is an add-on to behavioral support, not a substitute for it.
Smoking cessation carries a survival benefit, so delaying it forfeits that benefit. Tell: cessation is essential for every group from the start, not when symptoms are worse.
Unsupported attempts give up the gains of counseling, which identifies triggers and teaches coping strategies. Tell: the listed rule is that all cessation attempts are combined with counseling.

Correct. Every smoking cessation attempt should be combined with counseling, or behavioral therapy, which looks for triggers and gives coping strategies, to increase efficacy. Nicotine replacement, bupropion or varenicline can be added to that support.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: Which therapy is listed among those with a survival benefit in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: Inhaled corticosteroids reduce exacerbations in selected patients but raise pneumonia risk and are not on the survival list. Tell: the 3 survival therapies are cessation, long-term oxygen and noninvasive ventilation.
Long-acting antimuscarinics limit bronchoconstriction and help prevent exacerbations, but they are not listed as improving survival. Tell: oxygen for severe resting hypoxemia is.
The pneumococcal vaccine reduces community-acquired pneumonia but overall does not reduce deaths or admissions. Tell: the survival list is cessation, oxygen and noninvasive ventilation.

Correct. Survival benefits come from smoking cessation, long-term oxygen therapy for severe resting hypoxemia, and noninvasive ventilation for hypercapnic exacerbations. Symptoms and exacerbations guide drug therapy.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)/ chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD) for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
set2.q: When should palliative care be integrated for older adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: When the patient asks for it
Waiting for the patient to ask delays the planning that early integration provides. Tell: for older adults clinicians bring palliative care in early, with caregivers and advance directives.
Correct. For older adults palliative care is integrated early, with caregiver involvement and advance directives. For working-age adults it is introduced as the disease advances.
In the final weeks of life

Waiting until the final weeks loses the chance to plan with caregivers and advance directives. Tell: for older adults palliative care starts early. Late referral leaves little time for advance directives.

Palliative care is not a last resort after drug failure; for older adults it is integrated early alongside treatment. Tell: early integration with caregivers and advance directives is the listed approach.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: How is emphysema defined?
opts: Reversible bronchospasm is the hallmark of asthma, whose obstruction improves after a bronchodilator. Tell: emphysema's alveolar destruction is permanent, so its obstruction does not reverse.
Destruction and enlargement of the alveoli

Correct. Emphysema is an anatomic, pathologic definition describing destruction and permanent enlargement of the alveoli, with air trapping. That separates it from chronic bronchitis, which is defined clinically by chronic cough and sputum.

Chronic cough and sputum for at least 3 months a year over 2 years is the clinical definition of chronic bronchitis. Tell: emphysema is the one defined by pathology, the destroyed and enlarged alveoli, not by symptoms.
Narrowing of the bronchioles is small airway disease, a third component under the umbrella term. Tell: emphysema involves the alveoli themselves, which are destroyed and permanently enlarged.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: In the motivational framework of feedback, responsibility, advice, menu of options, empathy and self-efficacy, which element builds the patient's confidence in their ability to change?
opts: Correct. Self-efficacy focuses on enhancing the person's confidence in their ability to change and reinforcing belief in their own capabilities, for example by pointing to changes they have made before.
Feedback gives specific information about how the behavior is affecting the person's health, to raise awareness. Tell: confidence-building is the job of self-efficacy, the last element.
A menu of options presents a range of strategies so the person can choose what fits. Tell: offering choices is not the same as building belief in one's ability, which is self-efficacy.
Empathy acknowledges and validates the person's feelings and challenges with compassion. Tell: empathy accepts mixed feelings; self-efficacy reinforces confidence to act.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: Which patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease should be evaluated for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency as the cause?
opts: Upper-lobe, centrilobular emphysema is the smoking pattern. Tell: the deficiency pattern is panlobular and lower-lobe, which shows as basilar emphysema on the chest x-ray.

Correct. Patients under age 45, or those without significant smoke or particle exposure, should be evaluated for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Other suggestive features are predominantly basilar emphysema and a family history of emphysema.

Older heavy smokers fit ordinary smoking-related disease, the most common pattern. Tell: deficiency testing targets the atypical patient, one who is young (45 or under) or lacks a significant exposure.
Chronic bronchitis in a smoker is the usual exposure-driven disease and does not single out the deficiency. Tell: the deficiency causes panlobular emphysema in younger or unexposed patients.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: Which lung exam finding reflects a flattened diaphragm in this disease?
opts: Hyperresonance in emphysema is generalized from hyperinflation, not limited to one apex. Tell: the sign linked to the flat diaphragm is the lower intercostal spaces pulling in during inspiration.
Loud heart sounds at the apex
Heart sounds are distant and may be heard best at the epigastrium, not loud at the apex. Tell: the flattened-diaphragm sign is paradoxical lower intercostal retraction.
Neck veins that distend on inspiration
Jugular veins in this disease distend particularly during expiration. Tell: the flat-diaphragm sign is in the chest wall, with lower intercostal retraction on inspiration.

Correct. Paradoxical retraction of the lower intercostal spaces during inspiration reflects a flat diaphragm from hyperinflation. Other lung findings include decreased breath sounds in some areas with wheezing or crackles.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: Which symptom is an early sign of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in most cases?
opts: A barrel chest reflects established hyperinflation and is a physical finding, not the usual first symptom. Tell: the early clue is breathlessness with exertion and poor exercise tolerance.
Cyanosis of the lips or fingertips is an exam finding seen with poor oxygenation, more typical of advanced or bronchitic disease. Tell: the earliest sign in most patients is exertional dyspnea.
Clubbing is rare in this disease. Tell: an early sign that most patients share is breathlessness on exertion, while clubbing should prompt a look for something else.

Correct. Dyspnea on exertion, with exercise intolerance, is an early sign in most cases, and symptoms may be subtle at first. The disease then brings progressive dyspnea with chronic cough, wheezing and sputum production.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: Which is a goal of chronic management in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: Normal pulmonary function is an asthma goal, possible because asthma's obstruction reverses. Tell: this disease's obstruction is chronic and irreversible, so the goals are fewer symptoms, slower progression and fewer exacerbations.
Alveolar destruction in emphysema is permanent, so no therapy reverses it. Tell: smoking cessation can slow progression, but the damage already done stays.
Every patient should keep an albuterol inhaler to prevent or reduce symptoms, so removing it is not a goal. Tell: the goal is fewer symptoms and exacerbations, with rescue medicine still on hand.

Correct. The goals of chronic management are reducing symptoms and improving exercise tolerance and health status, preventing disease progression, preventing exacerbations, and reducing mortality. Long-acting bronchodilators and rehabilitation serve these goals.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: Which non-pharmacologic measure is essential for groups B and E but not listed as essential for group A?
opts: Correct. Smoking cessation is essential for every group, and groups B and E add pulmonary rehabilitation as essential; physical activity is recommended for all, and vaccines depend on local guidelines. Nonpharmacologic care is the foundation for everyone.
Smoking cessation, which can include drug treatment, is essential for every group, A included. Tell: the measure added for groups B and E is pulmonary rehabilitation.
Physical activity is recommended for all groups, not essential for B and E alone. Tell: rehabilitation is the measure that becomes essential with more symptoms or high risk.
Shingles vaccination, like pertussis and coronavirus vaccines, is listed as depending on local guidelines for every group. Tell: pulmonary rehabilitation is the essential addition for B and E.

set2.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
set2.q: Which process is listed as a contributor to airway remodeling and parenchymal destruction in this disease?
opts: Immunoglobulin E binding to mast cells is the allergic pathway of extrinsic asthma. Tell: this disease is driven by inflammation, oxidative stress and an imbalance between proteases and antiproteases.
Smooth muscle spasm that reverses describes asthma's bronchoconstriction. Tell: this disease causes chronic, irreversible obstruction through remodeling and destruction, not spasm alone.
Surfactant is not among the listed contributors. Tell: the 3 listed drivers are chronic inflammation, oxidative stress and protease-antiprotease imbalance.

Correct. Airway remodeling and parenchymal destruction are driven by chronic inflammation, oxidative stress and protease-antiprotease imbalance. That imbalance is also why a lack of alpha-1 antitrypsin, a protease inhibitor, destroys the lung.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: What does the BODE (body mass index, obstruction, dyspnea, exercise) index estimate?
opts: Home oxygen is decided by resting arterial oxygen or saturation thresholds. Tell: the index estimates 4-year survival.

Correct. The index adds points for body mass index, the 1-second volume, the dyspnea grade and the 6-minute walk distance; totals of 0 to 2 predict about 80% 4-year survival, falling to about 18% at 7 to 10 points.
The treatment group comes from symptoms and exacerbation risk and guides initial medicines. Tell: the index estimates long-term survival, not the group.
The airflow grade comes from the 1-second volume alone. Tell: the index combines 4 measures to predict 4-year survival. The grade is one ingredient of the index, not its output.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
set2.q: Which vaccine, given yearly, is proven to reduce hospitalizations and death in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: Correct. Every patient should get a yearly influenza shot, which is proven to reduce hospitalizations and death. The pneumococcal vaccine reduces community-acquired pneumonia but overall does not reduce deaths or admissions.

The pneumococcal vaccine reduces the incidence of community-acquired pneumonia, but overall it does not reduce deaths or admission rates, and it is not yearly. Tell: the yearly vaccine with proven mortality benefit is influenza.
Shingles vaccination is listed as depending on local guidelines, not as proven to cut hospitalizations and death. Tell: the vaccine every patient gets yearly is influenza.
Pertussis vaccination is also listed as depending on local guidelines. Tell: influenza vaccination, every year, is the one proven to reduce hospitalizations and death.

set2.q: What is the role of oral corticosteroids in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: Group B starts on a long-acting beta agonist plus a long-acting antimuscarinic. Tell: oral steroids are never chronic maintenance here; they are given for exacerbations.
Group A starts with a single bronchodilator, short- or long-acting. Tell: oral corticosteroids are reserved for acute exacerbations. Low-burden patients never need systemic steroids for maintenance.

After an admission the discharge bundle starts long-acting bronchodilators promptly and considers an inhaled corticosteroid if eosinophils are high. Tell: oral steroids treat the exacerbation, not the months after it.

Correct. Oral steroids are for acute exacerbations only in this disease, which is why they are missing from the list of common chronic therapies. Exacerbations are treated with antibiotics, bronchodilators, corticosteroids and oxygen.
